idiom_name: struct with sync.Mutex + sync.Cond (methods lock, defer unlock)
implementation_notes: Go has no per-object monitors, so the classic structure is a struct that holds a sync.Mutex together with the state, and methods that lock, defer mu.Unlock() and touch only the guarded fields; the Go wiki recommends exactly this for caches and shared state and warns against over-using channels because they look more idiomatic. Waiting uses sync.Cond, which is built from a Locker, waited on in a loop and signalled with Signal or Broadcast; for a fixed number of waiting consumers a buffered channel used as a counting semaphore is simpler. The language's doctrine points the other way when ownership can move: share memory by communicating, and replace the monitor with a channel-owning goroutine.
pitfalls: sync.Cond must never be copied after first use (go vet reports it) and Wait must run while holding the same Locker the Cond was created with, otherwise the unlock/wait pair is not atomic.
A mutex-guarded struct shares one lock across all methods: holding it across channel sends, I/O or callbacks serialises the whole object and hides lock-ordering deadlocks.
sync.Cond has no timeout and no cancellation; if callers must give up, model the wait with select on a channel instead, or the goroutine blocks forever.

variants.name: goroutine owning the state, methods as messages
variants.idiom_name: state-owning goroutine + request channel (share memory by communicating)
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of locking the object, one goroutine owns the state and every method call becomes a message - a closure, a request struct with a reply channel, or a select over several channels - so the owner processes calls one at a time; this is Go's preferred realisation of serialised method execution and the slogan share memory by communicating. There is no monitor lock and no condition variable: waiting is a goroutine blocked on a receive or a select, and the caller blocks on the reply. Choose it when callers can be asynchronous, when the object also owns a blocking resource such as a connection, or when the state is too complex to reason about under a lock; the cost is a channel hop per call and a goroutine that must be shut down explicitly.
pitfalls: The owning goroutine must be stopped explicitly (close(q.ops)) or it leaks; every request must carry exactly one reply or the caller blocks forever.
A panic inside the owner loop kills the object silently unless recovered, and a long-running operation inside the owner blocks every other method call.
Channel ownership does not compose with a mutex elsewhere: as soon as another path touches the state directly the serialisation guarantee is gone.
